reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Haemorrhoids are symptomatic enlargement and distal displacement of the normal anal cushions; the cushions themselves are physiological structures contributing to continence, so their mere presence is not pathological

Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and are typically painless, presenting with bright-red painless bleeding at defecation, mucus discharge, pruritus, and prolapse; external haemorrhoids lie below the dentate line and are somatically innervated, so become painful when thrombosed
The Goligher grading of internal haemorrhoids (grade I no prolapse, II prolapse with spontaneous reduction, III prolapse needing manual reduction, IV irreducible) guides management choice
Diagnosis rests on inspection, digital rectal examination, and proctoscopy; internal haemorrhoids are usually not palpable and are best seen on proctoscopy or anoscopy
First-line management is conservative: increased dietary fibre and fluid, stool softening, avoidance of straining and prolonged toilet sitting, and topical agents for symptom relief

Office procedures such as rubber-band ligation are effective for grade I to III disease, while excisional or stapled haemorrhoidectomy and haemorrhoidal artery ligation are reserved for higher-grade or refractory disease
Rectal bleeding must never be attributed to haemorrhoids without excluding proximal pathology, particularly colorectal neoplasia, in at-risk patients
Pregnancy, chronic constipation with straining, low-fibre diet, and raised intra-abdominal pressure are common contributory factors
reference.pathophysiology: The anal canal contains three main vascular cushions of submucosal connective tissue, smooth muscle (the muscle of Treitz), and arteriovenous communications that contribute to fine continence by sealing the canal. Haemorrhoidal disease develops when these cushions become engorged, hypertrophied, and prolapsed owing to deterioration of the supporting fibromuscular anchoring tissue, allowing distal sliding of the cushions. Repeated straining, prolonged defecation, chronic constipation or diarrhoea, and raised intra-abdominal pressure (as in pregnancy) increase venous congestion and shearing forces. Increased resting anal tone and arteriovenous shunting within the cushions contribute to the bright-red bleeding characteristic of internal haemorrhoids. Progressive fragmentation of the connective tissue and dilatation of the vascular plexus lead to bleeding, prolapse, mucus discharge, and, in external components, thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Colorectal carcinoma or rectal polyp causing rectal bleeding
Anal fissure (painful bright-red bleeding with sentinel tag)
Anal or perianal skin tag or hypertrophied anal papilla
Anal carcinoma or anal intraepithelial neoplasia
additionalInvestigations: Proctoscopy or anoscopy to visualise and grade internal haemorrhoids
Rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy to inspect the distal bowel
Colonoscopy where bleeding is unexplained, atypical, or the patient is at risk of neoplasia
Full blood count if bleeding is chronic or heavy, to detect iron-deficiency anaemia
Digital rectal examination to exclude a palpable mass and assess sphincter tone
Faecal immunochemical testing and further imaging where colorectal cancer must be excluded
redFlags: Change in bowel habit, weight loss, or iron-deficiency anaemia suggesting colorectal malignancy
Dark blood, blood mixed within the stool, or a palpable rectal mass
Persistent bleeding despite adequate treatment of visible haemorrhoids
Severe unremitting anal pain suggesting thrombosis, abscess, or another cause
New symptoms in older patients or those with a family history of bowel cancer
reference.prognosis: Most haemorrhoidal symptoms respond well to conservative measures and office-based procedures, with good long-term control; recurrence can occur, particularly if predisposing factors such as constipation and straining persist, and surgery carries small risks of pain, bleeding, and rarely incontinence or stenosis.
pitfalls: Attributing rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids without adequately excluding colorectal cancer in at-risk patients
Banding external or mixed haemorrhoids below the dentate line, which causes severe pain
Overlooking a coexisting fissure or fistula as the true source of symptoms
Neglecting to correct constipation and straining, leading to early recurrence
Aggressive circumferential excision risking anal stenosis
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on haemorrhoids
NICE clinical guidance on suspected lower gastrointestinal cancer referral
management: First-line conservative management with a high-fibre diet, increased fluids, stool softeners, and avoidance of straining and prolonged toilet sitting
Topical agents for short-term relief of pruritus and discomfort
Office-based rubber-band ligation for lower-grade internal haemorrhoids, with sclerotherapy or infrared coagulation as alternatives
Excisional or stapled haemorrhoidectomy or haemorrhoidal artery ligation for high-grade or refractory disease
Treat iron-deficiency anaemia arising from chronic or heavy bleeding
Exclude colorectal neoplasia with colonoscopy or faecal immunochemical testing when bleeding is atypical, unexplained or the patient is at risk
Correct persistent precipitating factors such as constipation and chronic straining to reduce recurrence
